passage: During Navratri, Minakshi's corner of the hostel room turned into a tiny shrine: a brass lamp (unlit, because of hostel rules), a marigold string, and her grandmother's old prayer book. She fasted nine days, eating fruit and sabudana from a steel box, even during lab exams. Her roommate Bhavna, who grew up in a family that didn't practise any religion, watched curiously. "Doesn't it get hard?" Minakshi smiled. "Yes. But when I read these lines, I can hear Aaji's voice. I feel like I belong somewhere." Bhavna asked if the fast meant she couldn't eat with the group on Friday. Minakshi thought. "I'll come and have fruit. I don't want to miss you either." Bhavna brought her a banana from the mess anyway.

qa.q: What was in Minakshi's corner of the hostel room during Navratri?
qa.a: A brass lamp, a marigold string and her grandmother's old prayer book.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel when she reads the prayer lines?
qa.a: She feels connected and at home, as if she can hear Aaji's voice and belongs somewhere.

qa.q: What choice helped Minakshi balance her fast with college life?
qa.a: She decided to join the Friday group and eat fruit, so she keeps her tradition without cutting herself off from friends.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see Minakshi's fasting?
qa.a: Bhavna is curious and respectful even though her own family doesn't practise any religion, and shows care by bringing a banana.

grounding: A young woman keeps a festival fast and family rituals in her hostel, finding belonging while fitting them alongside new friendships.

Dear Tarun,
You asked why I rushed home for Ganpati instead of the trek. I wish you could see it. Aaji still wakes at four to make modaks, and this year she let me fold them. Mine looked like crushed flowers, and she laughed so hard she had to sit down. Papa and I carried the idol home from the market on our shoulders, the same way his father did with him. When we sang the aarti together, all my college stress went quiet. There was one fight: I wanted a clay idol that dissolves in a bucket at home, not the painted one for the lake. Papa was upset at first. We settled on clay, painted by hand. Aaji said Bappa won't mind.
Nilesh

qa.q: What time does Aaji wake to make modaks?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel while singing the aarti with family?
qa.a: Nilesh felt calm and at peace, with all the college stress going quiet.

qa.q: What choice helped Nilesh honour tradition while bringing in a new idea?
qa.a: Nilesh talked through the clay idol idea with Papa, and they settled on a hand-painted clay idol, keeping the ritual while changing one part.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt about the clay idol request?
qa.a: Papa was upset at first, perhaps feeling the old way was being questioned, but he agreed once they found a middle path.

grounding: A young man keeps his family's festival rituals with devotion and finds belonging, while negotiating a new idea within the tradition.

passage: Ojas, you keep asking why I wake up at five on Sankranti when I'm twenty-one and could sleep. Let me tell you. In my family, on Sankranti morning, we walk to the river with my father, take a dip in the cold water, and come home to til-gul made by my mother. Then we fly kites from the roof until our fingers bleed. My friends in the city say it's old-fashioned, and sometimes I argue with my father about things like caste customs that I don't agree with. But this morning is different. When I hand til-gul to our neighbours and say, 'Speak sweetly,' I feel like a part of a long chain. I'm Harish, son of that river, and I'll keep going.

qa.q: What does the family walk to on Sankranti morning?
qa.a: They walk to the river with Harish's father.

qa.q: How does Harish feel when handing til-gul to the neighbours?
qa.a: Harish feels connected and proud, like part of a long chain of family and neighbours.

qa.q: How does Harish handle the tension between tradition and new ideas?
qa.a: Harish keeps the customs that feel meaningful, like the Sankranti dip and til-gul, while still arguing with his father about customs he disagrees with.

qa.q: What might Ojas understand after hearing Harish?
qa.a: Ojas might see that Harish isn't simply old-fashioned; the ritual gives Harish belonging, even while Harish questions other customs.

grounding: A young man describes keeping his family's Sankranti rituals with devotion for belonging, while questioning some other customs.

passage:
I'm Gautam, Jaya Didi's younger brother. She's twenty-one and studies physics in Delhi, and this year she came home to Patna for Chhath even though her exams were close.
She didn't just come for the food. She scrubbed the brass pots with Ma, shaped thekua with her own hands, and kept the fast with the women of the house, no water from the evening before. At the ghat, she stood in the river at sunset holding the soop with fruit and a lamp, eyes closed, lips moving.
Her college friends had teased her on video call. "A physics student standing in a river?" She laughed and said, "I know how the sun works. This isn't about that."
I asked her later why she bothered. She said, "When I'm here, I know exactly who I am."
I don't know everything she felt out there in the cold water. But she looked more peaceful than I've seen her all year.

qa.q: What did Jaya hold as she stood in the river?
qa.a: The soop with fruit and a lamp.

qa.q: What does Jaya's reply, 'When I'm here, I know exactly who I am,' suggest about what the ritual means to her?
qa.a: It suggests the festival makes her feel at peace and sure of who she is, a belonging her busy life in Delhi does not give, whatever her friends think.

qa.q: How did Jaya handle the tension between her friends' teasing and her tradition?
qa.a: She laughed it off and explained that her science and her ritual answer different questions, so she could keep both without quarrelling.

qa.q: How does Gautam see his sister at the ghat?
qa.a: Gautam is curious and not sure what she feels, but he sees her looking more peaceful than she has all year.

grounding: It shows, through a brother's eyes, a young woman who keeps a festival fast and ritual with devotion, finding belonging in it while living alongside new ideas.

Day one. The evening before the Ashadhi wari, Omkar, twenty, packed a cloth bag in his family's Pune flat: a white kurta, a small cymbal, his grandfather's old copy of abhangs. His college friend Tushar watched, puzzled. "You're walking with the pilgrims? You, the robotics guy?"
"Every year since I was eight," Omkar said. "With Baba. Two days."
Day two. On the road out of the city, thousands walked together, singing. Omkar's feet hurt. An old man he had never met shared his bhakri with him. When Baba started a verse his own father used to sing, Omkar's voice cracked. He felt, for a moment, part of something enormous and very old.
Day three. Back at the hostel, Tushar asked, "Don't you think all that's a bit outdated?"
Omkar thought for a while. "Some of it, maybe. I argue with Baba about some things. But when I walk, I'm connected to everyone who walked before me. I'm not giving that up."

qa.q: What did the old man share with Omkar?
qa.a: His bhakri.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's voice crack when Baba began the verse?
qa.a: The verse his grandfather used to sing moved him deeply, making him feel connected to his family and to something very old.

qa.q: How did Omkar respond to Tushar's question, and why is it a thoughtful answer?
qa.a: He admitted he questions some parts and argues with Baba, yet explained why he keeps the walk, holding tradition and new ideas together honestly.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Omkar differently after that conversation?
qa.a: Tushar might understand that the walk is about belonging and family for Omkar, not just old habit, even if Tushar doesn't share it.

grounding: It shows a young adult who keeps a family pilgrimage tradition with devotion, finding meaning and belonging in it while living with new ideas and questions.
